items.title: Vue/Nuxt → React incremental migration — architecture design and lead
items.meta: NOL Universe · Lodging partner B2B console · 7 legacy repos (543 items) + 10 new repos coexisting · 3 FE engineers
steps: The legacy codebase and the new React app had to coexist while we migrated without any service interruption. When I joined in 2022, this Vue/Nuxt stack was the very thing I had named as my weakness.

I wrote the migration strategy as an RFC first and reached team agreement. Instead of moving everything at once, Phase 0 laid the shared infra, auth and routing foundation, then domains were migrated one stage at a time.

nginx path routing and Istio VirtualService path splits gave the old and new apps a coexistence zone. Large migrations were split into Parts 1–4, pairing each new implementation with its legacy removal. The final Nuxt teardown was part of the upfront design.
Legacy PR share: 100% in 2022 → 69.4% in 2023 → 22.3% in 2024 → 6.5% in 2025 → 1.1% in 2026. Over four years, I saw through the migration off the stack I had named as my weakness.

items.short: Performance — verifying and rejecting an AI draft
items.title: Performance — verifying and rejecting an AI draft
items.meta: Mobile web · Redefining the bundling strategy
steps: A 3.44MB giant chunk was loading on certain pages. When I handed the analysis to an LLM, it concluded that React.lazy code splitting had cut the size dramatically.

I found the measurement limits the draft itself had noted: DOMContentLoaded and Load were identical before and after, and the draft admitted the results were "most likely cached". I re-compared keeping code splitting against a single bundle.

I rejected the AI's conclusion and redefined the problem. Instead of treating it as splitting versus monolith, I focused on the root cause of the excessive size. After removing the giant chunk I re-measured myself, accepted the trade-off of every page loading 1.71MB, and chose a single bundle because it was predictable.
Initial load 3.4MB → 1.5MB (55.9% reduction), DOMContentLoaded 346ms → 121ms, Load 487ms → 349ms. Evidence scope: client-side measurement on one mobile app.

items.title: Client log instrumentation DevTools · moving the cost of checking from code to the screen
items.meta: NOL Universe · 304 partner-console log definitions · wired into 4 domestic (MUI) and outbound (NDSP) apps · 0 new dependencies
steps: 304 log definitions were scattered across 10,000 lines of per-app generated code, with no way outside the code to see what was instrumented or what actually landed. Dead definitions, drift between senders and definitions (174 calling files) and StrictMode double-firing piled up.

I decided to move the cost of checking onto the screen. The inspector was built in vanilla DOM, independent of any app design system, so it dropped into both the MUI and NDSP app families, and collection changes were limited to one pilot screen to protect stored data.

By reverse-parsing the generated sender code I auto-generated five deterministic catalogs (human-readable md, detailed json, ingestion-check SQL, runtime meta, ref types). I built a dev-only inspector with a live firing feed, a 30-day real-volume overlay and a txtpb generation mode, plus an auto-firing runtime where a single tag line is all it takes to collect an event.

Auto-firing was verified byte-identical to the existing senders' payloads, and the production bundle grew only by a 96KB slim meta. The Databricks PAT was isolated behind a local dev proxy with 0 new dependencies, and the adoption and migration discussion was split into a convention RFC.

items.short: Standardizing the team's AI dev infrastructure
items.title: Standardizing the team's AI development infrastructure
items.meta: New in-house Claude plugin marketplace · 5 consuming repos
steps: Dev tooling was tied to the monorepo and the line between personal and team assets was blurry. Leaving installation to individuals risked dropping required rules.

I compared nine alternatives, four repo-bound and five shared, and documented each one's trade-offs and rationale. Because one bad change to a shared tool can block everyone, I laid the CI, permission and convention safety net first and added features after.
Adopted a two-axis structure: repo-bound assets under .claude/project-plugin with a gitignore whitelist, shared assets in a separate marketplace repo.
Launched the in-house marketplace with 8 plugins, applied it to 5 consuming repos and folded it into the onboarding docs.

items.title: Knowledge system redesign — moving to an LLM wiki
items.meta: Knowledge build pipeline for a large monorepo
steps: With one skill per domain, ten sessions on the same domain produced ten fragmented drafts.

I recorded three rejected alternatives with reasons: vector DB/embeddings (markdown plus grep was enough), hook auto-injection (false positives and complexity), and draft PRs (to keep automatic reviewer assignment).
Designed a three-way ADD/UPDATE/NOOP decision structure and a two-layer guard against self-replication.
Independent audit score rose from 0.52 (FAIL) to 0.87 (PASS), with evaluator scores of 93/85/90/92 and all 129 tests passing.

items.short: Overseas Partner Central — sales calendar architecture
items.title: Overseas Partner Central — sales calendar architecture · data transformation standard
items.meta: PC·Admin for overseas lodging partners · multi-language/multi-currency · 2 FE + PM, 2 BE, PPD, QA
steps: We had to build a new set of screens where overseas lodging partners manage rate plans, inventory and sales status. If shared policies such as currency decimal places and multilingual rate-plan labels were implemented per screen, every policy change would mean hunting through every screen.

I pushed shared policies down into lower FSD layers so screens only compose. The criterion was "keep the blast radius of a policy change narrow". The same principle applied to form and request transforms: a three-axis rule (role, location, shape), with an explicit boundary that passthrough requests get no wrapper.

Where no dedicated designer was assigned, I made several mockups, shared them with colleagues and adopted one from the feedback. The convention rollout was split into a 6-stage stacked PR, each stage passing type-check and lint. Since request objects are part of query cache keys, shape and values were preserved byte for byte so cache behavior never changed.

Calendar, base price and Daily Rate List now show identical occupancy pricing and cap values, and new features shipped behind feature flags without breaking existing operations. Convention compliance, 75–80% at the time of the survey, was normalized across the board.

standards.headline: Moving rules into the execution layer

items.title: Conventions enforced by tools, not documents
items.description: Documents that rely on being read don't get followed, so I pushed rules into the execution layer: ADRs moved into AI skills that apply automatically during work, repeated review comments became lint rules, and build and type checks became CI gates.

items.title: Conventions as skills — type-derivation rules · empty-value notation · table-cell navigation · frontmatter policy
items.description: Each convention became a skill instead of a document and was applied across the whole team at once. When a rule changes, only the skill changes.

items.title: Porting collaboration rules to new repos
items.description: CODEOWNERS, a PR template, 3 GitHub Actions workflows, 3 husky hooks and commitlint are set up in each new repo's first PR, so the rules are enforced from the first commit.

items.title: Policy split out of code into declarations · change points 11 files → 1
items.description: Sales-lock criteria were spread across 11 files, so changing one policy meant finding and editing every usage. I separated per-channel rules into policy declarations instead of code branches and gathered them in a single place; a rule change now ends with one declaration edit.

items.title: Removing triple-duplicated locale types — ~20 existing call sites untouched
items.description: The multilingual text type was defined in three places, so fixing one left the others out of sync. I unified them into a single definition with a module-augmentation slot pattern, designed so the ~20 existing consumers still compile unchanged.

items.title: E2E regression testing built where no tests existed
items.description: Beyond adopting Playwright, I standardized login sessions and data setup as fixtures so tests never rebuild preconditions (2,833 new lines). Core-flow regression checks run in CI before every deploy.

items.title: Removing an auth token exposed in the deployed bundle
items.description: A Sentry auth token was shipping inside the client bundle. A build-time-only value had leaked into the runtime artifact, so I separated the injection path and removed it from the bundle.
